forces: Soprano, two violins, viola and cello
performers: Carmel String Quartet; Rona Israel-Kolatt, soprano
intro: In Entrückung, the fourth movement of Schoenberg’s String Quartet No. 2, Op. 10, a soprano joins the four strings to sing Stefan George’s poem about leaving the earth. The harmony moves away from a home key and closes on an F♯-major chord.

sections.label: Intro · Chromatic string introduction, Sehr langsam
sections.mNote: Chromatic lines without a settled home key.

sections.label: B · Voice with string quartet
sections.mNote: Voice and four strings play five independent lines.

sections.label: C · Soprano, final stanza before string coda
sections.mNote: The soprano sings the end of George’s poem.

sections.label: Coda · Quartet after the voice
sections.mNote: The quartet plays on after the poem ends.

sections.label: Coda · F♯ major
sections.mNote: The four strings hold a major chord.

cues.title: Introduction, strings alone
cues.text: The strings begin alone, and their chromatic lines move away from a home key. Schoenberg described this introduction as a departure from earth, in which gravity loosens, the air grows thinner and earthly troubles fall away.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s Notes on the Four String Quartets, quoted in Therese Muxeneder’s work essay; the introduction’s harmony is discussed there. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Soprano entry, first line of George
cues.text: The soprano sings George’s first line, “Ich fühle luft von anderem planeten” — “I feel the air of another planet.” The voice enters among four independent instrumental lines.
cues.evidence: Stefan George, Entrückung, Der siebente Ring (1907), pp. 122–123; text and scoring reproduced in the Arnold Schönberg Center catalogue. Translation ours. https://archive2.schoenberg.at/compositions/werke_einzelansicht.php?werke_id=404&herkunft=allewerke
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: George’s poem Entrückung
cues.text: In George’s poem, friendly faces fade in the darkness. Trees and paths become unrecognisable, and the beloved’s shadow disappears. The speaker floats above ravines and clouds until only a spark of sacred fire remains.
cues.evidence: George, Entrückung (1907), complete German text in the Arnold Schönberg Center catalogue; this note summarises the poem as a whole. https://archive2.schoenberg.at/compositions/werke_einzelansicht.php?werke_id=404&herkunft=allewerke

cues.title: First performance, Vienna, 1908
cues.text: The Rosé Quartet and Marie Gutheil-Schoder gave the first performance at the Bösendorfersaal on 21 December 1908, before a hostile audience. In his later account, Schoenberg recalled laughter beginning in the scherzo and continuing through the two movements with soprano.
cues.evidence: Première date, hall and performers: Arnold Schönberg Center work catalogue. Audience account: Schoenberg’s introductory note for the Kolisch Quartet recording, Los Angeles, 1936–37. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10

cues.title: Instrumental coda
cues.text: After the poem ends, the quartet plays a long coda without the voice. The movement closes on an F♯-major chord.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s 1936–37 introductory note identifies the long instrumental coda: https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10. Hugh Wood, The Conservative Innovator (2001), confirms the F♯-major ending in the Chandos CHAN 9939 booklet: https://www.chandos.net/chanimages/Booklets/CH9939.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda at the première, Vienna, 1908
cues.text: In his introductory note for the Kolisch Quartet recording (Los Angeles, 1936–37), Schoenberg recalled that the audience at the first performance had interrupted even the soprano. After she finished, the four strings played the coda to the end without audible disturbance.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s introductory note for the Kolisch Quartet recording, Los Angeles, 1936–37, recalling the Vienna première of December 1908. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10

cues.title: Final chord, F♯ major
cues.text: The finale closes on a plain F♯-major chord of F♯, A♯ and C♯. The quartet began in F♯ minor.
cues.evidence: Hugh Wood, The Conservative Innovator (2001), and Charles Wilson’s accompanying essay describe the F♯-minor opening and F♯-major ending. Chandos CHAN 9939 booklet, PDF pages 5–6 and 8: https://www.chandos.net/chanimages/Booklets/CH9939.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The soprano joins the quartet
transitions.from: Intro · Chromatic string introduction, Sehr langsam
transitions.how: The soprano joins the strings over harmony that is not yet settled in a key. Her line sets George’s words against the quartet’s chromatic phrases, and the cello continues to move as one voice within the five-part writing.
transitions.evidence: Op. 10, fourth movement, introduction and first vocal passage; Therese Muxeneder’s discussion of harmony and vocal balance. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10

transitions.title: String coda after the soprano
transitions.from: C · Soprano, final stanza before string coda
transitions.how: After the soprano’s final phrase, the two violins, viola and cello continue alone in a long coda for strings only, which ends in F♯ major. Schoenberg described this coda in his introductory note of 1936–37.
transitions.evidence: Schoenberg describes the long string-only coda in his introductory note of 1936–37. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10

transitions.title: The final major third
transitions.how: The strings close on F♯ major. A♯ replaces the A♮ of the quartet’s original F♯ minor, and all four instruments play the final held chord together.
transitions.evidence: Hugh Wood, The Conservative Innovator (2001), describes the quartet’s F♯-minor opening and F♯-major close. Chandos CHAN 9939 booklet, PDF page 8: https://www.chandos.net/chanimages/Booklets/CH9939.pdf.

composer.epithet: Composer who abandoned tonality, continued to study Bach and Brahms, and wrote a minuet using all twelve notes.
facts: Largely self-taught; lessons with Alexander Zemlinsky
Alban Berg and Anton Webern from 1904; later Hanns Eisler and John Cage
Prussian Academy of Arts, Berlin, 1926–33; UCLA, 1936–44
Painter; author of Harmonielehre (1911); founder of the Society for Private Musical Performances
composer.background:
At the première of Pierrot lunaire in Berlin on 16 October 1912, Albertine Zehme stood onstage in a Pierrot costume. Behind a screen, five instrumentalists watched Arnold Schoenberg conduct. They had held twenty-five ensemble rehearsals to prepare thirty-odd minutes of music in which the voice slid away from its written notes, the flautist also played piccolo and the violinist also played viola.

Schoenberg was born in Vienna’s Leopoldstadt in 1874 and began learning the violin as a child. His father died when he was fifteen. From 1891 to 1895 he worked in a bank, making music with friends and teaching himself from scores. Alexander Zemlinsky, whom he met through the amateur orchestra Polyhymnia, gave him lessons. From Brahms he learnt how a small phrase could grow through continual change, and from Wagner how long the resolution of a chord could be delayed.
